title: Amelia Earhart's Life In Reverse | From a Pacific Search to a Kansas Porch
description:
Amelia Earhart's life is told backwards in this episode, opening on the radio messages of July 2, 1937, when her airplane disappeared on the way to Howland Island, and rewinding to her birth in Atchison, Kansas in 1897. The journey steps through the solo North Atlantic crossing of 1932, the yellow biplane she bought against advice, the hospital wards of Toronto in 1918, and the grandparents' house where she grew up. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the records arrive in reverse order and the person behind them appears before the fame. Dates, routes and radio messages follow the documented record, and theories about her disappearance are left as they are, disputed.

scenes.narration: No wreckage of her airplane has ever been found. In January 1939 a court in Los Angeles declared her legally dead, two years after she vanished. Divers, survey teams and writers have argued over the last hours ever since, and those explanations are still disputed. What is settled is the flight plan, the radio traffic and the empty sea that answered.

At 8:45 in the morning on July 2, 1937, a voice came through on the radio from her twin engine Electra. She said they were running north and unable to see the island, that the fuel was low, and that she could not raise the ship by radio. The Coast Guard cutter Itasca heard every word. Nothing further was ever received.

Three hours earlier, at 10 a.m. local time, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had lifted off from the dirt strip at Lae, in New Guinea, with about eleven hundred gallons of gasoline on board. Ahead lay Howland Island, a flat sliver of coral two thousand five hundred miles out in the Pacific, and no other landing place in between.

Three days before that, on June 29, 1937, the Electra had landed at Lae after a run across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. They had already covered roughly twenty-two thousand miles of the circuit. The crew replaced a faulty radio direction finder and waited for weather, knowing that the last stretch over open water was the hardest of the whole journey.

A month earlier, on June 1, 1937, they had departed from Miami, Florida, with the route reversed to run from west to east. The plan followed the widest part of the globe, with stops in South America, Africa, India and the islands to the north of Australia. She had fewer people with her than on earlier trips, and only Noonan as navigator.

Three months before that, in March 1937, her first attempt had ended on the ground at a naval air field near Honolulu. She flew the opening leg from Oakland in just under sixteen hours, but during the takeoff for the next stage the airplane swung off its path, the forward gear gave way, and both propellers struck the runway.

In July 1936 the new Lockheed Electra had been delivered, bought with fifty thousand dollars from a fund at Purdue University, where she advised women on careers and taught about aircraft. She called it her flying laboratory. The plane had extra fuel tanks and a new instrument panel, and she spent months with mechanics learning every system on it.

In the autumn of 1935 she had joined the staff at Purdue University in Indiana. Her title was counselor to women students, and she also advised the department of aeronautics. She lived in a residence hall on campus, gave talks across the state, and used the position to argue that women should train for paid work rather than accept the limits set for them.

Earlier that year, on January 11, 1935, she had become the first person to fly alone from Honolulu to the mainland, landing at Oakland after two thousand four hundred miles over water. She had a thermos of hot chocolate in the cockpit and drank it at eight thousand feet. The flight showed that the Pacific route could be flown by one pilot in one day.

In 1934 she had tried to earn money from fashion rather than flying. She opened a shop in a New York department store selling clothes with her name on them, and the venture closed before the year was out. That November a fire at her house in Rye destroyed many of her early papers, including poems she had written as a schoolgirl.

Four years before that, in February 1931, she had married George Putnam, the publisher who had handled her first book and her lecture tours. She kept her own name and her own flying. The marriage gave her an organizer for the business side of her life, and the two of them planned the records and the long flights together.

The women pilots she knew had begun to gather as a group in the years just before that, and they chose her as their first president. The organization was called the Ninety-Nines, after its founding members, and it still exists. She used the position to press for airfields, fuel and training that did not assume a pilot would be a man.

In 1930 she had set a women's world speed record of a little over one hundred and eighty miles an hour in a Lockheed Vega. The number mattered less to her than what it proved about women in the air. She spent that year on air races, lecture halls and magazine columns, and she was paid for all three.

In 1929 she had bought a Lockheed Vega with money from her writing and speaking, and then flown in a women's air derby from California to Ohio, coming third. She was thirty-one, and the racing circuit had women pilots competing over several days of cross country stages. The year before, she had become a national figure for reasons she disliked.

In June 1928 she had crossed the Atlantic as a passenger in a three engine Fokker called the Friendship, taking off from Newfoundland and coming down at Burry Port in Wales after about twenty-one hours. A pilot and a mechanic flew the aircraft. She had been asked because she was a woman who looked the part, and the press made her famous overnight.

She turned that fame into work in the months that followed. She wrote a book about the flight, toured the country to promote it, took a column writing about aviation, and appeared at fairs and schools. Reporters asked her what it felt like to cross the ocean, and she said plainly that the two men aboard had done the flying.

Before the fame, in 1925, she had worked at a settlement house in Boston, teaching and visiting families in the crowded districts. The job was respectable, low paid and steady, and she took it seriously. She was twenty-seven, she had left university without a degree, and flying cost money she did not have, so the evenings were spent on savings.

The year before that, in 1924, her parents had separated after years of difficulty, and she moved with her mother to Massachusetts. The family had moved house many times through her childhood, and the pattern had finally broken down. She and her sister Muriel had grown up watching the moves, and none of the three adults found them easy.

Three years earlier, on May 16, 1923, an international aviation body had issued her a pilot's license, the sixteenth given to a woman. She was twenty-five. The certificate was the proof she needed to fly for money and to enter races, and she kept it through the moves and the jobs that followed.

A year before that, in October 1922, she had flown her yellow biplane to fourteen thousand feet over California and set a height record for women pilots. The climb took her above the mountains in an open cockpit, and she came down with ice on her flying coat. The record was reported in the local papers and noticed by the aviation clubs.

Ten months earlier, in December 1921, she had passed her flying tests and received a license from the national aeronautic association, at a time when the federal government did not issue them at all. She had been flying for less than a year. Her instructor advised against buying her own aircraft, and she bought one anyway with money she had saved.

Six months before that, in the summer of 1921, she had paid about a thousand dollars for a second hand Kinner Airster, painted bright yellow, which she called the Canary. She learned to land it on a field outside Los Angeles. Her leather flying coat was new, so she slept in it and rubbed aircraft oil into it until the other pilots stopped laughing.

On January 3, 1921, she had taken her first lesson with an instructor called Neta Snook, one of the few women teaching flying in California. The contract covered twelve hours. To pay for it she worked as a telephone clerk, a photographer and a driver, and her mother put up part of the money against her own better judgment.

Two months before that, on December 29, 1920, she had gone up for the first time in a passenger plane over Long Beach, California, the day after watching a flying meeting with her father. The flight lasted ten minutes and cost ten dollars. She was twenty-three, and she knew on the way back to the ground that she would learn to fly.

Earlier that year she had left Columbia University in New York, where she had entered as a pre medical student in the autumn of 1919. The work did not suit her and she had no wish to spend her twenties in a laboratory. She went west to join her parents in Los Angeles, and her money was set aside for flying.

In the autumn of 1919 she had arrived in New York and enrolled at Columbia. She was the first member of her family to reach a university course. She studied for a few months, in a building of benches and bottles, before deciding that medicine was not the life she wanted, and she left without taking a degree.

A year earlier, in 1918, she had worked as a nurse's aide at a military convalescent hospital in Toronto during the last year of the war. She had left a finishing school near Philadelphia to do it. The wards kept her busy, and her time in the city also brought her to the edge of a flying field, where the aircraft were practising.

In 1916 she had gone to a finishing school outside Philadelphia, after finishing high school in Chicago. She was nineteen. She left in the middle of her second year, when a visit to her sister in Canada convinced her that the hospital needed her more than the school did, and she did not go back.

Through her school years the family had moved again and again because of her father's work, and she attended six high schools in four years before graduating in Chicago. She was a reader, a climber and a poor sitter. She later said that the only talent she had noticed in herself as a child was stubbornness, and she used it.

In 1907, at the age of ten, she had seen her first airplane at a state fair in Kansas City. The machine was slow, low and unimpressive, and she said afterwards that it looked like a box of wire and wood. Nobody in the crowd expected that the aeroplane would change anything, and neither did she.

Her childhood was spent mostly in her grandparents' house in Atchison, Kansas, a brick building with a wide porch, while her father travelled for the railroad companies and her mother's family stayed in the town. She and her younger sister Muriel climbed trees, collected birds' eggs, and went down the river. The family moved often, and the grandparents' house was the fixed point.

She was born on July 24, 1897, in that house in Atchison, Kansas, to Amy Otis and Edwin Earhart. Her grandfather was a judge in the town, and he had built the place himself. Her father worked as a lawyer for the railroads, and money came and went through her childhood, which was full of trains, suitcases and new school registers.
